question:
What is the largest integer that is a divisor of \[
(n+1)(n+3)(n+5)(n+7)(n+9)
\]for all positive even integers $n$?
solution:
The factors increase by 2. Modulo 3, the first three factors cover all three residues; modulo 5, all five factors cover all five residues, since 2 is coprime to both 3 and 5. Thus every product contains a multiple of 3 and a multiple of 5, so 15 divides every product.
To show no larger divisor always works, take \(n=2\). Its product is \(3\cdot5\cdot7\cdot9\cdot11=3^3\cdot5\cdot7\cdot11\). For \(n=64\), the factors are \(65,67,69,71,73\). None is divisible by 7 or 11, and only \(69=3\cdot23\) is divisible by 3. Hence the gcd of these two products is exactly \(3\cdot5=15\), and any universal divisor must divide it.
Final answer: 15
